cells.tense: You are carrying what people before you carried, and you are still handing it on.
cells.ask: Say one thing you were taught, out loud, to one person today — then leave it alone and let them keep it or not.
cells.core:
You're holding something heavy and you haven't gone stiff about it. That's the rare part. Most people either drop what they're holding or harden around it, and you've done neither — you're still passing things on while you stand under the weight.

What you hand over isn't a speech. It's the way you do a thing in front of someone until they can do it too. That only works while you keep adjusting it — keeping what's alive, letting the rest go. The weight is real. So is the fact that you still have room in you for someone else's hands. Keep both, and don't let the load close you off.
cells.sheetLine: You carry it and you still pass it on, adapted.
cells.verb: passing on what was handed down, alive and adapting
cells.place: under a load that has to keep being carried

cells.tense: You are bracing for a version of this where it finally gets done right.
cells.ask: Pick the one rule you enforce hardest and leave it unenforced once this week, and watch what actually happens without it.
cells.core:
You're holding the line harder than the line needs, and somewhere ahead is the version where it finally gets done right. So you grip. You correct the wording, you finish the sentence in their mouth, you make sure the right version gets through and the wrong one doesn't.

That grip is what's doing damage now. What you're protecting has stopped moving because you sealed it — and something that can't change can't be passed on. It just gets repeated. Take the rule you enforce hardest and leave it unenforced once. Not forever, not as a test. Just once, to see whether the thing you're guarding still stands without the pressure.
cells.sheetLine: You're guarding it so hard it can't move anymore.

cells.tense: You stood at a door a long time ago, and you are still standing there.
cells.ask: Write down one rule or habit from your family or your work that you actually keep, and why — a few lines, no audience.
cells.core:
Nothing came through that you could stand on, so you built your own way and called it being self-sufficient. It works. You get there on your own. But there's no framework under you that you trust enough to lean on, so each situation gets figured out from scratch and you're tired in a way rest doesn't touch.

The gap isn't effort — you have that. It's pattern. You can't see what's repeating because you didn't get handed a line to compare against. So look for the shape instead of a tradition. One rule you keep, one habit from your people, written down plainly, is enough to start seeing the mechanism underneath.
cells.sheetLine: No framework underneath you, so everything costs full price.

cells.tense: You are already the one people copy, and you have not once said so.
cells.ask: Name one thing someone has picked up from watching you, and say out loud that it came from you.
cells.core:
People around you are taking things from you without it being called teaching. A phrasing, a way of handling a difficult moment, a standard for when something is good enough — and it gets described as though it were simply how things are done here.

You're standing under a weight and holding steady, and that steadiness is the curriculum. Nobody had to sign up. It runs whether or not you claim it, and the part you're missing isn't the work — it's knowing you're the source. Say it once, plainly, about one thing. Not because you owe anyone a title. Because you're setting what gets kept, and right now you're doing it blind.
cells.sheetLine: You're already the source. You just haven't claimed it.
